steps.title: Hello
steps.how_to: How to choose between buongiorno, buonasera and buonanotte.
steps.intro: You'll learn which hello fits the hour, so you greet people right in the morning or the evening. You'll use it each time you walk into a bar, a shop or a restaurant.
steps.notice: Buongiorno is for the morning and early afternoon, and buonasera is for the rest of the day, even at 9 p.m. Buonanotte is what you say when someone is going to bed.
steps.context: Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m.

ask.said: Come saluti il barista alle dieci di mattina?
ask.en: How do you greet the barista at ten in the morning?

ask.said: Come saluti una signora in negozio alle cinque?
ask.en: How do you greet a lady in a shop at five?

ask.said: Un vicino va a letto. Cosa dici?
ask.en: A neighbor is going to bed. What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet the waiter with the right hello for the evening.

steps.title: How are you
steps.how_to: How to say how you are with sto.
steps.intro: You'll be able to answer 'how are you?' the way people here do. You'll say it every time a shopkeeper or a neighbor asks.
steps.notice: The question and the answer use the same word: sta or stai when you ask, sto when you answer. To say you're well, say 'Sto bene'.

ask.said: Come stai?
ask.en: How are you?

ask.said: Un negoziante ti dice: «Come sta?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: A shopkeeper says, “How are you?” What do you say?

ask.said: Ciao! Come stai oggi?
ask.en: Hi! How are you today?

mission.goal: Say you're well and ask the shopkeeper back.

steps.title: Be polite
steps.how_to: How to greet and ask after someone with tu or Lei.
steps.intro: There are two ways to say 'how are you?': one for friends and one for shopkeepers and older people. You'll use them every time you greet someone here.
steps.notice: With a friend you say 'come stai' and 'e tu'. With a shopkeeper or an older person you say 'come sta' and 'e Lei'. When you're unsure, use Lei until they offer tu.

ask.said: Vedi un amico. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You see a friend. What do you ask?

ask.said: Un amico ti dice: «Ciao, come stai?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: A friend says, “Hi, how are you?” What do you say?

ask.said: Una signora anziana ti dice: «Come sta?» Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: An older lady says, “How are you?” What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet the barista politely and ask how they are.

steps.title: Name
steps.how_to: How to give your name and ask for someone else's.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say your name and ask for someone else's. It's the first thing people say when they meet.

examples.said: Mi chiamo Kate. E Lei, come si chiama?
examples.en: My name's Kate. And what's your name?
Nice to meet you. My name's Rosa.
My name's Tom. Nice to meet you!

steps.notice: Mi chiamo and then your name is how you say who you are. To ask, start with come: 'Come si chiama?' with Lei, 'Come ti chiami?' with a friend.

ask.said: Come ti chiami?
ask.en: What's your name?

ask.said: Ti chiami Marco?
ask.en: Is your name Marco?

ask.said: Vuoi sapere il nome di una signora. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want to know a lady's name. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Give your name and ask a neighbor's name.

say.said: Mi chiamo …. E Lei, come si chiama?
say.en: My name's …. And what's your name?

steps.title: Where you're from
steps.how_to: How to say where you come from and where you live now.
steps.intro: You'll be able to tell people where you come from and that you live here now. People here ask it early, often the first time you meet.

examples.en: No, I live here, in Florence.

steps.notice: Where you come from starts with sono: sono americano, sono di Chicago. Where you live now starts with abito: abito qui, abito a Firenze. A woman says americana; inglese stays the same for everyone.
steps.context: 'Di dove sei?' is one of the first things Italians ask, because where you come from matters a lot here.

ask.said: Sei italiano?
ask.en: Are you Italian?

ask.said: Di dove sei?
ask.en: Where are you from?

ask.said: Dove abiti?
ask.en: Where do you live?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor where you're from and that you live here.

say.en: I'm American, from …. I live here.

steps.title: Time here
steps.how_to: How to say how long you've been here.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say how long you've been here. It's a good answer when someone is curious about you.

examples.said: Da quanto tempo è in Italia?
examples.en: How long have you been in Italy?

examples.said: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
examples.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
How long have you lived here?
I've lived here for a month.

steps.notice: Italian says it in the present: the verb, then da and the time, as in sono in Italia da tre settimane and abito qui da un mese. The time is still going, so it stays in the present.

ask.said: Da quanto tempo sei in Italia?
ask.en: How long have you been in Italy?

answer.en: I've been in Italy for … weeks.

ask.said: Da quanto tempo abiti qui?
ask.en: How long have you lived here?

ask.said: Sei qui da un anno?
ask.en: Have you been here for a year?

answer.en: No, I've been here for … months.

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor how long you've been in Italy.

say.said: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
say.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.

steps.title: When you're lost
steps.how_to: How to say you didn't understand and ask someone to say it again.
steps.intro: These are the phrases you'll use most in your first weeks. You'll say them at a counter, a stall or a ticket window whenever someone speaks too fast.

examples.said: Può ripetere più piano, per favore?
examples.en: Could you say that again more slowly, please?

examples.said: Scusi, non ho capito. Può ripetere?
examples.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. Could you say that again?

examples.said: Non ho capito. Può ripetere, per favore?
examples.en: I didn't understand. Could you repeat that, please?

steps.notice: Non ho capito says you didn't get it, and può ripetere asks them to say it again. Add più piano when you want it slower.
steps.context: Asking for più piano, per favore is normal here, and most people are pleased you're trying.

ask.said: Hai capito?
ask.en: Did you understand?

ask.said: Il cassiere parla troppo veloce. Cosa dici?
ask.en: The cashier is talking too fast. What do you say?

answer.said: Scusi, non ho capito. Può ripetere?
answer.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. Could you say that again?

ask.said: Il farmacista ripete, ma è ancora veloce. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: The pharmacist says it again, but it's still fast. What do you ask?

answer.said: Può ripetere più piano, per favore?
answer.en: Could you say that again more slowly, please?

mission.goal: Ask the vendor to repeat the price more slowly.

say.said: Scusi, non ho capito. Può ripetere?
say.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. Could you say that again?

steps.title: Got it
steps.how_to: How to say you understood what was just said.
steps.intro: This short phrase shows that something has clicked. You'll say it when someone has explained or repeated something for you.

examples.said: Ah, ho capito! Un caffè, allora.
examples.en: Oh, got it! An espresso, then.

steps.notice: Ho capito means you got it, about something just said. People check with ha capito?, or hai capito? with a friend.

ask.said: Hai capito?
ask.en: Did you get that?

ask.said: Il cassiere ripete il prezzo, piano. Cosa dici?
ask.en: The cashier says the price again, slowly. What do you say?

ask.said: Il farmacista ripete più piano. Cosa rispondi?
ask.en: The pharmacist says it again more slowly. What do you say?

mission.goal: Say you got it after someone repeats something.

steps.title: Ask for a word
steps.how_to: How to ask what a word means or how to say something in Italian.
steps.intro: These two questions help you learn new words on the spot. You'll use them when you meet a word you don't know at a counter or in a shop.

examples.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.notice: Learn these as ready-made questions: cosa vuol dire for a word you heard, come si dice for a word you need. Say them just like this and add the word.

ask.said: Non conosci una parola. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You don't know a word. What do you ask?

ask.said: Cerchi la parola italiana per “receipt”. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You need the Italian word for “receipt.” What do you ask?

answer.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

ask.said: Il barista dice «resto». Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: The barista says “resto.” What do you ask?

mission.goal: Ask how to say a word in Italian.

say.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.title: Order one or two
steps.how_to: How to order one or two of a drink or a snack.
steps.intro: You'll be able to order one of something for yourself, or two when you're with a friend. You'll use it every time you order at the bar.

examples.said: Un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
examples.en: A cappuccino and a croissant, please.

examples.said: Allora, due cappuccini e due cornetti?
examples.en: So, two cappuccinos and two croissants?

examples.said: Una spremuta e due caffè, per favore.
examples.en: A fresh juice and two espressos, please.
So, two sandwiches and an orange soda.

steps.notice: For one, say un or una with the item: un caffè, una spremuta, un'aranciata, and uno spritz. For two, say due and change the last letter, -o to -i and -a to -e, while caffè stays the same: due cappuccini, due spremute, due caffè.

ask.said: Sei al bar da solo. Cosa ordini la mattina?
ask.en: You're at the bar alone. What do you order in the morning?

ask.said: Sei al bar con un amico. Cosa chiedi da mangiare?
ask.en: You're at the bar with a friend. What do you ask for to eat?

ask.said: E dopo pranzo, cosa chiedi per voi due?
ask.en: And after lunch, what do you order for the two of you?

mission.goal: Order two coffees for you and a friend.

steps.title: Order politely
steps.how_to: How to order with vorrei or prendo.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say what you'd like at the counter or the table. You'll use it at the bar, at the restaurant and anywhere you order.

examples.en: Good morning! What are you having?
Good evening! What are you having?
I'll have a sparkling water, thanks.

steps.notice: To order, start with vorrei, I'd like, or prendo, I'll have, and add what you want. When someone asks cosa prende? or cosa prendi?, prendo is the natural answer.
steps.context: Cappuccino is a morning drink; after lunch Italians order an espresso.

ask.said: Sei al bar. Cosa prendi?
ask.en: You're at the bar. What are you having?

ask.said: Fa caldo e hai sete. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: It's hot and you're thirsty. What do you ask for?

answer.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice.

ask.said: Vuoi anche un po' d'acqua. Cosa dici al barista?
ask.en: You also want some water. What do you say to the barista?

answer.said: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
answer.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

mission.goal: Order a drink politely at the counter.

say.said: Vorrei una spremuta d'arancia, per favore.
say.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice, please.

steps.title: How much
steps.how_to: How to ask the price of one thing or of several things.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what something costs, whether it's one item or a few. You'll use it at the market, in shops and at the newsstand.
steps.notice: Ask quanto costa for one thing and quanto costano for several, with the thing after it. The answer often starts the same way: costa due euro, costano tre euro.

ask.said: Vuoi il giornale. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want the newspaper. What do you ask?

ask.said: Al mercato guardi le pesche. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: At the market you're looking at the peaches. What do you ask?

ask.said: Al bar guardi i cornetti. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: At the bar you're looking at the croissants. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Ask the price of something at a stall.

steps.title: Hear a price
steps.how_to: How to understand and say a price in euros and cents.
steps.intro: You'll be able to catch a price when the cashier says it, and say one back. You'll hear prices at every till, stall and ticket window.
steps.notice: A price is the euros, then e and the cents, so quattro e cinquanta is 4.50, and euro stays the same for any amount. Before uno and otto the tens lose their last letter: ventotto, trentuno.

ask.said: Quanto costa un caffè al bar?
ask.en: How much is an espresso at the bar?

ask.said: Quanto costa un cappuccino?
ask.en: How much is a cappuccino?

ask.said: Quanto costano un caffè e un cornetto?
ask.en: How much are an espresso and a croissant?

mission.goal: Say the price back to the cashier to check it.

steps.title: Card or cash
steps.how_to: How to ask if you can pay by card or cash.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask if you can pay the way you like. You'll use it at every checkout and market stall.

examples.said: Sì, certo, può pagare con la carta.
examples.en: Yes, of course, you can pay by card.

steps.notice: Posso pagare asks if you can pay, and then you add how: con la carta or in contanti. The answer you hear back is può pagare.
steps.context: Shops take cards, but small shops and market stalls often prefer cash for small amounts.

ask.said: Hai solo la carta. Cosa chiedi alla cassa?
ask.en: You only have your card. What do you ask at the register?

ask.said: Al mercato non hai la carta. Cosa chiedi?
ask.en: At the market you don't have your card. What do you ask?

ask.said: Hai il bancomat. Cosa chiedi alla cassa?
ask.en: You have your debit card. What do you ask at the register?

answer.en: Can I pay with my debit card?

mission.goal: Ask to pay by card at the till.
